Assembly

REV D front shell + rear cover

Ghosted — where everything packs in

The printed parts at 22% opacity, every bought part solid. A section answers “what is at this plane”; the question a builder asks is “what is in there, and does it all fit”.

⚠ The exploded drawing is one revision behind

cad/exploded.py still lays out a 114 alloy plate at balloon 33 and a pair of 100 × 40 strip heatsinks at 34. Neither part exists: there is no alloy plate, and the heatsink is one 150 × 74 × 10 block. Balloon 33 has no BOM row — ignore it, and read 34 as the single block. Everything else in the view is current. Listed under open items.

What the box actually is now

Shell 335 × 178 × 22 with an 11 mm brim, cover 335 × 178 × 6. Two identical 82 × 125 × 37 bays stand off the cover — Pi stack at x-102, buck at x+102 — so the unit is 65 deep over a bay and 72 over the fan shroud, which is the number that matters when it swings.

The controls moved out of a column beside the screen into a row under it, at 70 mm pitch. That is the whole of rev C: the control strip became height instead of width, the shell came inside the 350 mm bed, and it prints as one piece, face down, no supports. Bezel is 18 at the sides and 18 top.

Nothing is cooled inside. There is 13.5 mm behind the panel and no room for a fan or an inner sink in it. Everything thermal happens on the outside of the cover — see the thermal path below, including the part of it that is honestly weak.

Why the split is this way round

The front shell is one piece (face + walls) and the rear cover is a flat plate whose 22 screws thread into the shell’s rear brim. Nothing is bolted on from the front.

It is better in four ways beyond looks: the front A-surface prints face-down so it is bed-smooth, the seal groove lands on a flat brim rather than on a wall, the joint sits at the back out of the weather, and every precision feature — aperture, bond land, control bores — sits on one part.

The 8 M3 holes around the aperture are DELETED — do not drill them

They clamped the alloy heat plate to the outside of the cover. There is no alloy plate. The heatsink’s own base closes the aperture from the inside, so every one of those eight would now be a through-hole in the weather face into the sealed cavity, held shut by nothing.

Two of them were worse than redundant: at 30 mm pitch the pair at x ±30 had their bores crossing the aperture edge at 30, cutting into the 8 mm sealing land the heatsink is bonded to — the one surface the whole thermal joint depends on. The other pair was cut entirely inside the aperture, i.e. in air, which is why the ring looked harmless in every render.

The fans mount in the shroud, not in the cover: 2 × 80 mm IP67 on eight pads behind the louvred face, their four screws each also clamping the mesh. The only fixings that reach the cover are the 4 shroud bosses, and those stop in blind pilots 4.5 mm deep. Nothing new goes through the plate.

Sensor positions — all four, on the cover’s inner face

They used to stand inside the two board bays, and those bays are now hollowed right through to the inner face — so every one of them was standing on a floor that no longer exists. They sit in the top and bottom bands instead, which is the only inner face that is neither a bay nor the heatsink seat. Coordinates are shell coordinates; the cover mirrors in y.

BoardCentre4 × M2.5 Ø2.2 at
MCP23017(-100, +68)±19.05 x, ±6.35 y
MCP9808(+100, +68)±10.16 x, ±6.35 y
ADXL345(+100, -68)±10.16 x, ±6.35 y
ICM20948(-100, -68)±10.16 x, ±6.35 y

Standoffs are 1.5 mm, so board + standoff is 3.1 mm against the 13.5 mm behind the panel. Every one is checked against the cover’s sealing face, and the whole inner face is checked against the panel envelope rather than against a list of other cover features — which is what finally caught the old GPS cradle driving 1047 mm³ through the display.

The encoder and all four keys run through the MCP23017, which is why it is the one board that has to be near the control row. I²C polling dropping quadrature counts is not a problem here: your code already uses a dedicated fast poller separate from the 1 Hz sampler, and the encoder runs at 3 V.

The mount is a bail, and it hangs on nothing but the cover

No dash tilt bracket, no detent, no VESA. It is a Simrad-style bail: a base plate flat on the dash and two arms rising either side, pivoting at mid-height on trunnions grown from the rear cover. Bail base 327 × 96 × 8; arm eyes r18 on the trunnions’ r15 lands.

Grown from the cover, not bolted to it. A separate bracket needs screws through that plate, and every one of them is a hole in the pressure boundary the 3 mm cord is there to seal. The trunnions sit inside the bezel width at x ±156 against an edge at 168, with the arm faces at ±160 and 7 mm of arm outboard of that — exactly to the bezel line, no further.

Why mid-height. The old bottom hinge put the assembled CG 114.7 mm above the axis, which made the unit a pendulum on it — 12.4 N·m at 6g, and that is the number that forced a detent crown. The axis now runs through the CG height at y+8.7, so the moment falls with the lever instead of being fought with hardware, and hand-set friction is enough.

The interface is a 316 serrated washer pair, not plain friction. Inside the bezel width the disc cannot grow, and plain friction tops out under 1.4× for any size that fits — a bigger disc grips harder but lengthens the lever by the same amount. Interlocking teeth hold mechanically, roughly 10× a friction face, so holding no longer depends on a friction coefficient nobody has measured. All 316 through the joint, and Tef-Gel the threads: 316 galls on 316, and a nut in a plastic pocket is a textbook crevice.

How high it sits. The base plate lies flat on the dash under the unit and the arms rise from it vertically — that is what a bail is. The axis lands 131 mm above the plate, and that height is solved, not chosen: tilt swings the unit’s corners DOWN, and at 20° the lowest corner of the real envelope — cover, bay bumps, and the fan shroud 44 mm behind the cover — reaches 121 mm below the axis, so the arms carry that plus 10 mm of air under it. Top edge of the unit sits 211 mm above the dash at rest; the axis is 50 mm behind the front face.

The arms do not lean. Leaning them puts the plate behind the unit instead of under it and adds a bending moment at every foot bolt, and it buys nothing — the clearance that matters is height. Base fixes with 6 Ø5.5 × 10 slots in two rows 68 apart, so the rows take the peel moment; the arm feet take 4 M5 fore-and-aft, which is what resists each arm rotating about its own foot.

Tilt runs one way: 0° to 20°, face UP. That is the price of the arms staying inside the bezel width. They run at x 160–167 while the cover is 335 wide, so they share the unit’s own footprint and can only do it by staying behind the cover. Tilting the face up swings the bottom edge forward, away from them — probed clear across the whole range. Tilting it down swings that edge into the blades: 1,487 mm³ at 5°, 16,174 at 20°. Face-up is the direction a dash display below eye level is tilted anyway, so this is a range and not a consolation — but face-down would need the arms outboard of the bezel, and that is the constraint you set.

Three parts, not a U — for orientation, not for bed size. At 334 mm a one-piece U would fit the 350 bed; what it could not do is lie flat, because the base is horizontal and the arms are vertical. Split at the feet, each part prints flat in its strongest orientation and nothing is in cross-layer bending.

Cable entry, vent and coax all face DOWN, in blocks beside the bumps. They used to be on the cover’s flat face, and they could not be: the two bay bumps own that face from |x| 58 to 146 and are hollowed right through, so two of the three bosses were built inside a void, fused to a bay wall by whatever part of them happened to overlap it. Outside the bays and inside the seal the flat face has a 10 mm strip and a 15 mm band left; the smallest of these fittings needs 19.

The face is full — the part is not. Each bump stops at |y| 62.5 while the cover runs to 89.2, so beside each bump end there is a pocket 88 wide × 13.5 deep × 37 tall with nothing in it. A block fills the two bottom pockets and the three bores run horizontally through it and exit downward: no standing water, no sun on a nylon gland, an automatic drip loop on the cable, and zero cost in width or depth because nothing reaches past the bumps’ back plane. Every seat and every nut is in open air with the cover on the bench, which is when you fit them.

The teardrops stop 3 mm short of each face. A horizontal bore’s crown sags, so each has a 45° apex above it — but an apex is a notch, and run full-length it cut a V-groove straight across the flange’s O-ring land on all three. The last 3 mm is round crown, which the tap trues anyway, and the build now probes a thin annulus at each face and refuses to export if it is not solid all the way round.

4 tie-wrap anchors on the cover’s inner face, 2.2 mm slots for a standard 2.5 mm tie. They are on the cover because that is where the harness runs — the boards, the sensors and the gland are all on this part, and you dress cables before closing it up.

Still open

Touchscreen driver board is not placed. The DROK buck has the +x bay; the touch controller still needs its outline, hole pattern, and which edge the display ribbon and the HDMI/USB connectors leave from.

PiCAN-M footprint and N2K connector position. The Pi bay is sized for the stack, not for where the N2K plug wants to come out of it.

The internal air-to-metal step is unproven. See the thermal path — it is the one number on this build nobody has measured, and the fallback is drawn but not bought.

Antenna — still wants a ground plane

🚨 The HYS is a handheld whip, designed to work against a radio body and your hand as a counterpoise. On a plastic box it will show poor SWR and mediocre receive. For real AIS or VHF work, run the pigtail out to a proper marine antenna — the bulkhead is the right interface either way.

⚠ GPS is an external puck now, so the old RF problem — a transmit whip 26 mm from a GPS patch — is gone with it. What is left in the box is display-ribbon noise at L1 and into the SDR: the foil shield is still worth doing, and it must be bonded to system ground. Ungrounded foil does almost nothing.

Measured parts

redrawn from your photos — please check

Correction — I misread the display sketch

I read 133 mm as a hole pitch. It is not: both 133 and 26.5 are measured to the right edge, so those two bottom bosses are 106.5 mm apart. I then derived a 307.5 mm module width from that mistake and called it corroboration for an assumed 305. Both retracted — the sketch does not give the module width at all.

The drawing above is redrawn with your datums: right edge for 133 and 26.5, bottom edge for 30 and 13, top edge for 8.25. It is settled now by measurement, not by that derivation: module 310 × 131 × 12.

The aperture is cut to the measured panel

Active area measured 295 × 112, against a derived 292.5 × 109.7 — 2.5 narrow and 2.3 short. Had that gone to print it would have masked a strip of pixels down two edges.

The aperture is 300 × 121, and it is set by the bond band rather than by the active area: the module is 310 × 131 and the silicone needs a flat land, so the aperture is that outline less 5 mm a side. What shows in the extra is the module’s own black border, not housing. It clears the active area by 2.5 mm a side.

The panel is located, not just glued: a rail across the bottom it rests on and pads down each side, with the top left open so it goes in bottom-edge-first and swings home. Tight on all four and you would have to slide glass straight down through a wet bead. The seat is checked by pushing the panel past its fit in each direction and requiring the shell to push back — a rail that merely clears at nominal has located nothing.

Both big parts fit the bed now

They did not: at the old layout the shell was 389 × 193 against a 350 × 350 bed, which no rotation fixes, and it had to be printed in halves and bonded across the front face. Moving the control strip from beside the screen to under it turned width into height, where there was room to spare.

Shell 335 × 178 and cover 335 × 178: one piece each, flat, 7.5 mm a side to spare in x. The bail base is the next biggest at 327, which is also why it is three parts rather than a U.

Where the measurements landed

Driver board is complete. 113.25 × 55.25 × 17, four Ø3.5 holes for M2.5 at TL (9.00, 3.75), TR (109.25, 3.75), BL (9.00, 48.00), BR (109.25, 51.50), origin top-left. The pattern is not rectangular — left pair 44.25 apart, right pair 47.75. A symmetric standoff set would not have fitted. It stands in the +x bay, which is 37 mm deep for exactly this.

Display rear is complete too. Five standoffs, not six — no top-centre. All Ø8 base, M3 × 5 deep. The cover picks up 4 of them: the centre one is under a board bay, and any post landing inside the heat aperture is dropped rather than printed as a loose island.

Panel depth 12 mm is what sets the shell at 22: face 2.5 + panel 12 leaves the 13.5 mm that everything on the cover’s inner face has to live inside.

The seal

shell brim → rear cover

As modelled

Groove3.60 W × 1.61 D
Cord3 mm round rubber
Squeeze~46%
Path±159.9 × ±81.7
Cord length955 mm
Brim face11 mm
Groove to inner lip1.60 mm
Groove to bolt1.20 mm web
Bolt to outer edge2.00 mm
Fasteners22 × M3 × 16
Assembled gap0 — metal to metal

How it works

  • A cord in a groove closes metal-to-metal. The cover lands flat on the brim face and the cord is squeezed into its groove — the assembled gap is zero, where the old foam band held the cover 1.5 mm off. The display posts derive their length from that, so they moved with it
  • Groove is in the shell’s brim; the cover is a plain flat land. Cutting it into one part only is what keeps the joint self-aligning, and the brim face prints as a solid top surface — the best finish FDM gives
  • The screws sit OUTBOARD of the cord, so nothing is punched through the seal. The shell’s pilots are blind and never reach the cavity, which makes the leak path the cover’s through-holes — hence a bonded sealing washer on every one
  • Depth 0.54 × cord, width 1.20 × cord — fills ~78% of the groove, leaving room for the squeezed cord to spread
  • The brim is 11 mm because five bands have to fit across it: land 2.00 + M3 2.6 + web 1.20 + groove 3.60 + lip 1.60. The build fails if that stops adding up
  • The Gore vent removes the pressure term, so this seal only has to stop water, not hold a differential
  • Splice the cord with a scarf joint and CA, positioned away from the bottom rail
  • ✓ Cord measured at 3 mm — the listing said both 3 mm and 3/32″ and they are 0.6 mm apart. It is the 3. The groove as drawn is correct and does not move

Why a cord and not the foam band

The foam band was the previous answer and it is gone. The reason is plain: the cord is what is in the box on the bench, and flat closed-cell foam sheet in the right thickness is something you have to go and source. A seal you own beats a seal you have to find.

It is also the easier of the two here. The cord is narrower than the 3.60 band it replaces, so the brim gets more lip, not less — and a cord captured in a groove cannot roll out of the joint as the cover goes down, which a loose band can.

Hinged visor

REV D helm_visor_revD.stp

As modelled

Hood294 wide, 22 deep
Pivot span296 mm, x ±148
Pivot landr5.5–10.5 annulus
Pivotfriction on a 1.0 mm 316 shim, 2.73 N·m the pair
Pivot boltM5 316 + nyloc, in the visor ear
Mass in ASA83 g

Two decisions worth knowing

  • Friction, not detent teeth — the crown is gone from both joints. Teeth were the honest answer to a 6.19 N·m moment on the old bottom hinge. Nothing on this part carries that: it is set by hand, it has no steps to land between, and its failure mode is slipping rather than splitting an ear
  • What makes the friction hold is the 316 shim, not ASA on ASA. Like-on-like stick-slips and polishes as it works, so the setting drifts. The shim runs free between the two printed lands, giving ASA/316 on both faces — and the two faces are in series, so the stack slips at whichever is weaker and only one face carries the torque. Counting both is how this calculation gets inflated 2×
  • No side wings, and the bevel is structural. On two pivots the hood is a 296 mm cantilever. A bare flat plate has I = 373 mm&sup4; and flexes 15 mm under a 20 N push; the 45° turned-down bevel lifts that to 953 mm&sup4; and 6 mm. Stress is SF 5 either way — the bevel is about how floppy it feels
  • Pivot faces mesh at 0.00 mm — upstands and ears verified coincident
  • Range is set by the housing; say if you want it to fold flat to the screen at rest

Fan shroud

104 × 168 × 38 box · 44 behind the cover

Two 80s, not one 120 — and the louvres are the whole back

The heatsink is 150 × 74: narrow and tall. A single 120 round was covering a square area over a strip and wasting most of its swept circle on shroud wall. Two 80s cover 160 of the 150.

The outer face is one louvred rectangle — 29 slats at 45°, no round bores, no divider between the fans. Each slat’s outboard edge is its low edge, so water that lands on it runs out and drips off; at 45° with the pitch equal to the height there is no straight line of sight through the stack at all. Get that sign wrong and the louvres become gutters that funnel spray into the fan.

These louvres are the only opening in the back. Air leaves through side louvres with 45° awnings over them and through a 3-bay slot along the low edge — which is the drain as much as it is exhaust. Without it this part is a tray holding salt water against the heatsink’s glue line for the life of the boat.

⚠ The shroud lands over four brim screw heads and that is deliberate: shrinking it to clear them does not work, because two 80 mm fans span 160 exactly, and moving those four screws leaves a 104 mm gap in the fastener ring across the middle of the long edge. The shroud is relieved for the heads instead — a rain shield can afford four pockets; the pressure boundary cannot afford a gap in its clamp.

LP-24 shroud · all dimensions mm

Subassemblies

the things a whole-unit render cannot show

A render of the finished unit answers “what does it look like”. It does not answer “where does that go” or “which way round does it fit”, which are the questions that come up with a part in your hand. Each view below exists because a specific question had no picture.

The thermal path — and the step that is honestly weak

One heatsink, 150 × 74 × 10, bonded base-out into a 3 mm recess in the cover’s inner face. Its base is flush inside; 4 mm of fin stands proud outside through the 59 × 135 aperture, under the shroud, in the fans’ airstream. There is no alloy plate and no conduction block: the heatsink’s own base closes the aperture, which takes a part, an interface and 6 mm out of the stack.

The recess walls index the block while the adhesive cures, so the gluing jig is gone too. Trim the fins back 8 mm all round first — a bought extrusion carries fins to the edge of its base, and without that band there is no flange to seal or glue against.

⚠ The bottleneck is inside the box, not outside it. With the fins pointing out, the interior sees a bare flat plate 111 cm², and getting watts out of the internal air and into that plate is natural convection plus whatever the Pi’s own fan stirs. The fans, the fins and the shroud are all working on the easy half of the problem. This is the one number on the build that nobody has measured.

The fallback, if it throttles: a second finned block bonded to the inside of that same base. The offcut from trimming this one’s sealing land is very nearly the right part. The alternative orientation — fins inward — is not available: there are 13.5 mm behind the panel and the display screws need them.

The Pi is the other source and it is handled differently, because it is a long way from anything metal and already carries its own cooler. In a sealed box that fan exports nothing — but it stirs, which lifts internal convection from roughly 4 to 15–20 W/m²K, and that term is exactly the one in the way.

Print notes

ASA blue · 0.4 nozzle · 0.2 mm · enclosure on. Perimeters 5 on the shell and cover, 4 elsewhere. Infill 40% gyroid on the shell, cover and bail arms, 25% elsewhere. This page used to say a flat “5 perimeters, 30% gyroid”, which contradicted the build manual’s slicer card on both counts — the manual is the one you print and stand at the machine with, so it wins and this now matches it. Every part prints flat-face down with no supports — the shell face-down on the bed, the cover bays up, the shroud on its louvred face, both bail parts flat. Slice from 3MF at High refinement.

About 1.55 kg across 8 parts, at 1.07 g/cm³: Front shell 280 g · Rear cover 530 g · Visor 83 g · Fan shroud 134 g · Bail base 263 g · Bail arm 44 g x2 · LP-24 shroud 158 g · Strain clamp 16 g. The fit coupon is extra — and print it first.

Print helm_encoder_coupon_revA before anything else. 9.8 cm³, about twenty minutes. Two Ø9.7 bores: one through a 2.5 mm floor (the real shell face) and one through a 5.0 mm pad, which brackets the 5.08 mm the measured 8 mm bushing can clamp. Thread the encoder into the 2.5 station with its nut and lockwasher and you have proved the face.
